verifications.claim_text: metalinguistic codes were effective for enhancing learners' immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during text revision
verifications.evidence_quote: although direct corrections and codes were effective to enhance learners’ immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy (i.e., during text revision), a long-term advantage (i.e., four weeks after feedback provision) was only evident for direct corrections
verifications.explanation: The claim's central proposition — that metalinguistic codes enhanced learners' immediate grammatical accuracy during text revision — is directly supported: the abstract states that "direct corrections and codes were effective to enhance learners’ immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy (i.e., during text revision)," and the results section reports that both metalinguistic groups (ME+G, p = 0.009; ME+GN, p < 0.001) significantly outperformed the control group on grammatical errors successfully corrected during revision. The peripheral proposition about non-grammatical accuracy is also supported: ME+GN significantly outperformed the control group (p < 0.001) on non-grammatical errors successfully corrected. The population (low intermediate EFL writers) and the timing/scope (immediate, during revision) are likewise stated in the source. No assertion is contradicted and no hedge is removed, so the claim is verified.

verifications.claim_text: a mental-effort measure of cognitive load was significantly lower when learners processed direct corrections targeting grammatical issues, implying that metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands
verifications.evidence_quote: A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues.
verifications.explanation: The central assertion is stated almost verbatim in the abstract: "A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues." Section 5.4 confirms the underlying contrast: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and Table 3 reports "***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]". The peripheral interpretive assertion (metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands) is also supported by the discussion: "it is plausible that the problem-solving nature of the metalinguistic CF types may have placed more attentional demands on learners than the explicit provision of correct forms of the direct CF ones, which may have in turn increased their cognitive load". No assertion is contradicted and no peripheral assertion is absent, so the claim is verified.

verifications.claim_text: teachers provided feedback on both higher-order and lower-order concerns despite using Grammarly as a complement, with no division of labour
verifications.evidence_quote: The findings showed that teachers provided feedback both on global and local aspects of writing despite using Grammarly as a complement, and there was no division of labor such as that a teacher takes care of higher-order and Grammarly takes care of lower-order concerns.
verifications.explanation: The claim's central proposition — that teachers provided feedback on both HOCs and LOCs despite using Grammarly as a complement — is stated almost verbatim in the abstract ("The findings showed that teachers provided feedback both on global and local aspects of writing despite using Grammarly as a complement") and in the findings ("all six participants provided feedback on both HOCs and LOCs, despite having Grammarly feedback on LOCs as a complement"). The peripheral proposition of "no division of labour" is likewise stated in the abstract ("there was no division of labor such as that a teacher takes care of higher-order and Grammarly takes care of lower-order concerns") and in the discussion ("there is no division of labor, such as that AWE takes care of LOCs ... and a teacher takes care of HOCs"). No assertion is contradicted and no hedge is removed, so the claim is verified.

verifications.claim_text: a mental-effort measure of cognitive load was significantly lower when learners processed direct corrections targeting grammatical issues, implying that metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands
verifications.evidence_quote: A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues.
verifications.explanation: The central assertion is stated almost verbatim in the abstract: "A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues." Section 5.4 confirms the underlying contrast: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and Table 3 reports "***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]". The peripheral interpretive assertion (metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands) is also supported by the discussion: "it is plausible that the problem-solving nature of the metalinguistic CF types may have placed more attentional demands on learners than the explicit provision of correct forms of the direct CF ones, which may have in turn increased their cognitive load". No assertion is contradicted and no peripheral assertion is absent, so the claim is verified.

verifications.claim_text: teachers provided feedback on both higher-order and lower-order concerns despite using Grammarly as a complement, with no division of labour
verifications.evidence_quote: The findings showed that teachers provided feedback both on global and local aspects of writing despite using Grammarly as a complement, and there was no division of labor such as that a teacher takes care of higher-order and Grammarly takes care of lower-order concerns.
verifications.explanation: The claim's central proposition — that teachers provided feedback on both HOCs and LOCs despite using Grammarly as a complement — is stated almost verbatim in the abstract ("The findings showed that teachers provided feedback both on global and local aspects of writing despite using Grammarly as a complement") and in the findings ("all six participants provided feedback on both HOCs and LOCs, despite having Grammarly feedback on LOCs as a complement"). The peripheral proposition of "no division of labour" is likewise stated in the abstract ("there was no division of labor such as that a teacher takes care of higher-order and Grammarly takes care of lower-order concerns") and in the discussion ("there is no division of labor, such as that AWE takes care of LOCs ... and a teacher takes care of HOCs"). No assertion is contradicted and no hedge is removed, so the claim is verified.
